(b) Arch pipe foundation. For arch pipe foundation, unless otherwise indicated, pipe shall be laid in trenches and on foundations prepared as selected by the contractor in conformance with the bedding class, trench width and depth, as recommended by the manufacturer's published data.
(c) Definition of pipe foundation terms. Pipe foundation terms are defined as follows:
Class B bedding may be achieved by either of the following two construction methods:
(1) Shaped bottom with tamped backfill. The bottom of trench excavation shall be shaped to conform to a cylindrical surface with a radius at least two inches greater than the radius to the outside of the pipe and with a width sufficient to allow six-tenths of the width of the pipe barrel to be bedded in fine granular material fill placed in the shaped excavation. Place and compact backfill shall be placed and compacted at sides of pipe to a thickness of at least 12 inches above top of pipe. Use of this bedding method shall be limited to trenches with firm bottom and sides.
(2) Compacted coarse granular bedding with a tamped backfill. Pipe shall be bedded in compacted coarse granular material placed on a flat trench bottom. The thickness of granular bedding must be at least one-fourth the outside pipe diameter, but not less than four inches thick under pipe barrel, and extend at least halfway up the pipe barrel at the sides. Compacted backfill shall be carefully placed above the granular material up a minimum depth of 12 inches over the top of pipe.
Class C bedding may be achieved by either of the following two construction methods:
(1) Shaped bottom. Pipe shall be bedded with ordinary care in an earth foundation formed in the trench bottom by a shaped excavation which fits the pipe barrel with reasonable closeness for a width of at least 50 percent of the outside pipe diameter. Place compacted fill to a minimum depth of six inches above top of pipe.
(2) Compacted coarse granular bedding with a tamped backfill. Pipe shall be bedded in compacted granular material placed on a flat trench bottom. Thickness of granular material must be at least four inches under the barrel and must extend one-tenth to one-sixth of the outside diameter up the pipe barrel at the sides. Compacted backfill shall be placed above the granular material to a minimum depth of six inches over top of pipe.
Trench depth means the vertical distance from pipe invert or flow line to finished ground surface.
Trench width means the horizontal distance between trench walls at any point from one foot above top of pipe to trench bottom.
(Ord. No. 2005-09, app. B(02770, pt. 3), 4-25-2005)

(1) Tunnel liner—12 inches to 42 inches. For tunnel liners 12 inches to 42 inches, contractors shall:

When the average head on the test section is greater than three feet, the allowable leakage shall be multiplied by the ratio of the square root of the average test head over the square foot of the base head of three feet.

The maximum allowable leakage limit is 50 gallons/(inch of internal diameter)(mile of sewer)(day) when the average head on the test section is six feet or less. When the average groundwater head on the test section is greater than six feet, the allowable leakage shall be increased in proportion to the ratio of the square root of the average groundwater head over the square root of the base head of six feet.

(2) At all other locations, contractors shall install service tubing by trenching and backfilling, unless otherwise noted.
(3) Contractors shall lay tubing at depth dictated by field conditions, but with not less than 18 inches cover.
(4) Contractors shall bed tubing on firm soil. Remove any rocks, masonry, or any other objectionable material, which could damage tubing.
(5) Contractors shall lay tubing in compliance with manufacturer's recommendations.
(6) Contractors shall restore ground surface to original condition. Replace or repair any damaged improvements.
(Ord. No. 2005-09, app. B(02710, pt. 3), 4-25-2005)
1462:
All pipe connections shall be made with standard factory-fabricated fittings except where special connection details, if any, are shown on drawings.
(Ord. No. 2005-09, app. B(02710, pt. 3), 4-25-2005)
1463:
The following regulations shall apply for installing water pipe in tunnel liner:
(1) For tunnel liner four inches or smaller, contractors shall insert water tubing into tunnel liner using methods, which prevent damage to tubing.
(2) For tunnel liner six inches to 42 inches, contractors shall:
a. Insert water pipe concentrically into tunnel liner by securing hardwood blocks radially or PVC-coated steel spacer around water pipe at no more than ten-foot longitudinal intervals. Use steel banding for securing wood blocks in place.
b. Blow sand into annular space, between water pipe and tunnel liner; starting at the longitudinal center and proceeding outward to each end. Use techniques, which assure complete filling of all voids from the liner invert up to or near the top of the water pipe.
c. Use water main pipe in tunnel liner with push-on joints or, at the contractor's option, use mechanical joint type provided the contractor coordinates actual tunnel liner size to provide at least one inch clearance all around pipe joint gland outside diameter.
d. Restrain pipe and fittings at each end of tunnel liner in accordance with section 71-672, pertaining to anchorage requirements.
(3) For tunnel liner 48 inches and larger, contractors shall:
a. Use the following procedure for installing water pipe in the tunnel when adequate working room is available; otherwise follow same procedures as specified for tunnel liner, six inches to 42 inches.
b. Insert water pipe into the tunnel liner after having grouted the bottom of the tunnel to exact grade required to support the pipe in proper position.
c. Permanently secure the water pipe in position by blocking each pipe length at the top and sides with brick and mortar, followed by bedding the water pipe to a depth equal to one-fourth the pipe outside diameter, with concrete.
d. Plug the ends of the tunnel with 12-inch thickness of masonry, leaving weep holes at the lower end of the tunnel.
(Ord. No. 2005-09, app. B(02710, pt. 3), 4-25-2005)
1464:
The following regulations shall apply to valves, fittings and hydrants:
(1) Contractors shall provide valves, fire hydrants, fittings and other appurtenances as indicated on the drawings, specified herein, and as requested by the city. Comply with applicable provisions of AWWA C600.
(2) Contractors shall set fire hydrants plumb and with ground line index within 0.1 foot of actual final ground level.
(3) Contractors shall set valves and valve boxes plumb, with valve box cover level with surface. Set lower section of valve box concentric with valve operating stem. Avoid contact at lower end of valve box with valve body or pipe.
(Ord. No. 2005-09, app. B(02710, pt. 3), 4-25-2005)
1465:
The following regulations shall apply to anchorages:
(1) Nondirect burial locations. Piping/anchorage support materials for nondirect burial locations shall be as follows:
a. Contractors shall install hangers and support in accordance with MSS SP-69 and SP-80.
b. Contractors shall install metal tie rods and bands in accordance with the requirements of AWWA C 600 for thrust restraint, using components as shown in NFPA 24.
(2) Direct burial locations. For direct burial locations, contractors shall:
a. Anchor all bends, valves, tees, fire hydrants, reducers and other points of unbalanced pressure as necessary to resist thrust at test and working pressures, with suitable allowance for water hammer. Also, anchor the piping system installed on steep slopes where gravitational force might otherwise cause piping displacement. Accomplish piping system anchorage by use of concrete reaction bracing, metal tie rods and bands, and/or restrained joint systems. When using concrete reaction bracing, pour concrete against firm earth and allow it to cure for at least five days before placing main under pressure. Position concrete blocks of sufficient size to counteract the magnitude and direction of the resultant thrust force.
b. Accomplish fire hydrant assembly anchorage by use of metal tie rods and bands and/or restrained joint systems. Keep joints and hydrant drain openings clear and accessible. Provide special support blocks at plastic pipes according to manufacturer's recommendation. When using bands and tie rods in conjunction with reaction bracing, provide a separate band for each tie rod. Use corrosion-resistant materials throughout. When using restrained joint systems, utilize methods and place these special joints at appropriate fittings and pipe joints in accordance with manufacturer's recommendation.
c. Anchorage detailed on drawings, if any, represents minimum anchorage to be installed. Field conditions may require additional anchorage, and it is the contractor's responsibility to recognize such additional requirements and to provide appropriate additional anchorage.
(Ord. No. 2005-09, app. B(02710, pt. 3), 4-25-2005)
1466:
Where constructing on piers, supporting pipe on bridges, or for other special work, contractors shall use safe and generally accepted construction methods to accomplish the required work.
(Ord. No. 2005-09, app. B(02710, pt. 3), 4-25-2005)
1467:
(a) Cast iron and ductile iron mains. Contractors shall install three-fourths and one-inch size corporation stops directly into tapped holes in the water main. Use service saddles for all taps larger than one inch size.
(b) PVC mains (four inches and smaller only). Contractors shall use service saddles for all service taps.
(Ord. No. 2005-09, app. B(02710, pt. 3), 4-25-2005)
1468:
Contractors shall install pipe detection tape in trench, approximately two feet above pipe. Contractors shall provide pipe detection tape for all nonferrous water mains unless otherwise noted.
(Ord. No. 2005-09, app. B(02710, pt. 3), 4-25-2005)
1469:
(a) Contractors shall avoid permitting dirt, rubbish, construction materials, etc., to enter lines and appurtenances during construction. Use whatever means are necessary to obtain a clean and internally smooth system prior to final acceptance.
(b) Contractors shall limit use of flushing water to rates and quantities, which will not interfere with, service to water customers.
(Ord. No. 2005-09, app. B(02710, pt. 3), 4-25-2005)
1470:
(a) General leakage requirements. Contractors shall make the entire water line system as near watertight as practicable. Contractors shall eliminate all detectable leakage regardless of test results hereinafter required.
(b) Testing. To test for water leakage, contractors shall:
(1) Furnish and use appropriate test equipment and methods. Include gage, meter, pump and connections.
(2) Bleed all air from the system prior to testing, providing any necessary corporation stops and piping installations.
(3) Pressure test all elements of the piping system. Where piping is buried or otherwise concealed, maintain the pressure test for not less than six hours. Visible piping may be tested for a lesser time period, if approved by the city. Conduct pressure testing at 200 psi unless a lower pressure is recommended by a manufacturer of an element of the system. When a manufacturer does recommend a lower test pressure, furnish the city with a detailed written explanation before commencing test work. In no event may the lower test pressure be less than 110 percent of the nominal working pressure of the pipe comprising the system. Measure pressure for testing referred to the elevational datum of the lowest pipe of the line section being tested.
(4) Where possible, use methods and perform construction work in such sequence as necessary to accomplish pressure testing as work progresses. Do not pressure test more than a one-mile length of pipe at one time. Provide temporary piping and accessories if required to isolate test sections.

1471:
Contractors shall comply with the following procedure for disinfecting:
(1) Chlorinate all potable water lines on completion of construction, after flushing and prior to placing in service. Use precaution to prevent backflow to supply system. Comply with AWWA C 651, including section 9 procedures on final connections to existing mains. At the contractor's option, accomplish chlorination by the tablet method, the continuous feed method, or the slug method.
(2) Fill lines with potable water containing sufficient chlorine to show a chlorine dose of at best 25 mg/l for the tablet method, a ten mg/l minimum residual at the end of 24 hours retention period for the continuous feed method, or a 50 mg/l minimum residual at the end of three hours of exposure for the slug method.
(3) Provide and operate all equipment and provide all materials necessary for disinfecting water mains. Draw off at taps and hydrants along the line until a DPD test or approved chlorine test kit shows a strong indication of residual chlorine.
(4) Retain chlorinated water in the system for a period of 24 hours for either tablet method or continuous feed method. Test for specified residual. If residual is as specified or greater, flush the system with potable water, otherwise repeat entire procedure until satisfactory results are obtained. If the slug method of disinfection is used, dispose of heavily chlorinated water in a manner acceptable to Federal, state and local environmental regulatory agencies.
(5) Demonstrate lines to be free of contamination by drawing samples there from on two successive days in the presence of the city. Deliver samples to a qualified laboratory for examination. On receipt of satisfactory test report from the foregoing laboratory, and with the approval of the city, the lines so tested are to be considered free of contamination and placed in service. In the event contamination persists, resterilize as necessary until receipt of satisfactory test report. All costs of disinfecting and bacteriological tests are to be paid by the contractor.
(Ord. No. 2005-09, app. B(02710, pt. 3), 4-25-2005)
1475:
(a) Tunneling pertains to the installation of carrier pipe or tunnel liner below ground by means other than open cut excavation. The extent of tunneling is shown on the drawings in article X of this chapter.
(b) Tunnel liner sizes indicated on the drawings in article X of this chapter and elsewhere in the contract documents are minimum nominal diameters. Use appropriate size and type of tunnel liner and construction methods as necessary to provide a complete tunnel liner installation.

(1) Route clearing, division 9 of this article.

(3) Water system, division 6 of this article.
(4) Sanitary sewer system, division 5 of this article.
(5) Storm sewer system, division 4 of this article.
(Ord. No. 2005-09, app. B(02408, pt. 1), 4-25-2005)
1476:
(a) Traffic control. Contractors shall schedule and conduct work in a manner, which will minimize inconvenience to vehicular and pedestrian traffic. Provide flaggers, barricades, warning signs, warning lights, and other warning means as appropriate. Maintain traffic on all roads and streets, which must be crossed by utility lines. All traffic controls during construction must conform to Part VI of the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices, ANSI D 6.1e.
(b) Weather limitations. Contractors shall conduct all operations during weather conditions appropriate to the work being performed.
(Ord. No. 2005-09, app. B(02408, pt. 1), 4-25-2005)
1477:
Quality assurance shall comply with applicable provisions of the following codes and standards, unless otherwise indicated:
(1) AASHTO, Standard Specifications for Highway Bridges, section 16 "Specification for Steel Tunnel Plates".
(2) AISC, "Specifications for the Design, Fabrication and Erection of Structural Steel for Buildings" including, the commentary.
(3) AREA, Manual for Railway Engineering, section 4.12 "Specification for Steel Tunnel Liner Plates."
(Ord. No. 2005-09, app. B(02408, pt. 1), 4-25-2005)
1480:
Where carrier pipe is installed without tunnel liner by tunneling methods, conformance with carrier pipe material specifications is required unless otherwise indicated.
(Ord. No. 2005-09, app. B(02408, pt. 2), 4-25-2005)

a. Steel pipe tunnel liner, four inches and smaller. Conform to ASTM A 53 material specifications. Use galvanized steel, Schedule 40 minimum, with threaded couplings.
b. Steel pipe tunnel liner, larger than four inches. Conform to ASTM A 53 or A 139 material specifications, except hydrostatic testing is not required. Join pipe sections with full strength, continuous welds in accordance with procedures approved by the American Welding Society to obtain a watertight seal.
c. Thickness requirements. Unless otherwise indicated on the drawings, contractors shall use pipe meeting the following thickness requirements:

(Ord. No. 2005-09, app. B(02408, pt. 2), 4-25-2005)
1482:
Where carrier pipe is installed in tunnel liner and mining methods are utilized, contractors shall comply with the following specifications:
(1) Materials. Contractors shall:
a. Fabricate tunnel liner sections of corrugated steel plate especially manufactured for tunnel liner service. Design liner sections and fasteners in consideration of tunnel location shown on the drawings. For liner plate design purposes, use soil, wheel, and surcharge loads of sufficient magnitude to insure a safe liner plate system in actual use conditions.
b. Provide tunnel liner plate having a minimum thickness of 0.179 inches and liner plate fasteners having a minimum diameter of 0.625 inches.
(2) Fabrication. Contractors shall:
a. Generally. Tunnel diameters shown on the drawings are in terms of the required minimum clear inside diameter of the erected liner plate tunnel. Fabricate liner plate sections so as to allow complete installation from within the tunnel, and with alternate liner plate rings in the erected tunnel containing two threaded grout holes in the vicinity of the tunnel invert and two grout bleed holes in the vicinity of the tunnel crown.
b. Galvanized coating. After tunnel liner plate sections have been formed, punched, etc., hot dip galvanize plate sections with at least a two-ounce coating of spelter per square foot total for both sides. Galvanized liner plates must not be warped, and the spelter coating must be free from defects such as blisters, flux, abrasion, poor adhesion and uncoated spots.
c. Bituminous coating. After galvanizing, fully coat both sides of liner plate sections with an asphaltic bituminous coating not less than 0.05-inch thick and conforming to AASHTO N 190 for bituminous protected corrugated metal pipe.
(Ord. No. 2005-09, app. B(02408, pt. 2), 4-25-2005)
1483:
For vent piping, contractors shall:
(1) Conform to ASTM A 53 or A 120 material specifications. Use two-inch minimum Schedule 80 steel pipe with butt-welded joints for vent construction.
(2) Provide enamel primer and two coats exterior enamel paint in color selected by the city for above grade piping.
(Ord. No. 2005-09, app. B(02408, pt. 2), 4-25-2005)
1484:
The following regulations shall apply to accessories:
(1) Grout. Grout shall be one part Portland cement; two parts masonry lime; four parts mortar sand; two percent of an approved admixture of Bentonite, Septamin Stearex, or Hydrocide Liquid; and where required, a retardant. Use sufficient mixing water that will produce a workable mixture of grout capable of being pumped into the voids created by the tunneling.
(2) Concrete. Contractors shall use 2,000 psi compressive strength concrete.
(3) Clay brick. Clay brick shall be ASTM C 32, Grade MS or ASTM C 32 sewer and manhole brick or ASTM C 216 facing brick, Grade MW or SW, of nominal size 8 x 2¼ x 3¾ inches. Color and texture as selected by the contractor.
(4) Concrete brick. Concrete brick shall be ASTM C 55, Grade P-II, of nominal size 8 x 2¼ x 3¾ inches; gray-white concrete color with smooth formed natural texture.
(5) Mortar.
a. Materials. Mortar materials shall consist of the following:
1. Cement. Cement shall be Portland cement ASTM C 150, Type I or II.
2. Sand. Sand shall be ASTM C 144, well screened, clean, hard sharp, siliceous, free from loam, silt and other impurities. Provide the following grain size distribution:
(i) No. 10 sieve, passing 95—100 percent.
(ii) No. 50 sieve, passing 15—40 percent.
(iii) No. 100 sieve, passing 0—10 percent.
(iv) Removal by decantation 0—5 percent.
3. Water. Water shall be clean, fresh, free from oil, acid, organic matter and other deleterious substances.
b. Mix proportions. Contractors shall provide mortar mixed in the proportion of one part cement to three parts sand with only enough water to allow good workability of the mix. Hydrated lime may be added in amounts not exceeding ten percent of the cement weight.
(Ord. No. 2005-09, app. B(02408, pt. 2), 4-25-2005)
1487:
Contractors shall examine areas and conditions under which tunneling is to be done, and notify the city in writing, of conditions detrimental to proper and timely completion of work.
(Ord. No. 2005-09, app. B(02408, pt. 3), 4-25-2005)
1488:
(a) Contractors shall carry out work in a safe manner, taking all necessary precautions and measures necessary to maintain a stable construction system, which does not weaken existing earth or structures nor cause settlement of the over passing roadway or railway section.
(b) When tunneling operations are carried out under railroad tracks, highways, streets, or any other existing thoroughfare, contractors shall perform operations in such manner as not to interfere with nor in any way endanger the normal operation of such thoroughfares.
(c) Contractors shall complete all tunneling work at one particular location before starting work at another location.
(Ord. No. 2005-09, app. B(02408, pt. 3), 4-25-2005)
1489:
The following requirements are supplemental to the excavation section of this article:
(1) When required, contractors shall excavate suitable pits or trenches for tunneling operations. Contractors shall provide all necessary bracing, sheeting and/or other temporary means to insure safety of persons and property.
(2) Contractors shall maintain excavation free from water, mud and debris, which will interfere with an efficient tunneling operation. Neatly dry-excavate material of whatever nature encountered within the tunnel. Sluicing or jetting excavation techniques shall not be used.
(3) Contractors shall limit excavation to the minimum diameter required for tunnel liner installation.
(4) Contractors shall pressure grout all excessive voids, which may develop about the tunnel liner exterior.
(5) Contractors shall promptly backfill all pits and trenches.
(Ord. No. 2005-09, app. B(02408, pt. 3), 4-25-2005)
1490:
(a) When installing tunnel liner by the jacking method, contractors shall use guide rails or other jacking frame structure to effectively maintain tunnel liner at proper line and grade. Tunnel liner shall be forced into place with suitable jacks, which apply uniform pressure around the tunnel liner end section. Contractors shall excavate at the lead end of the tunnel as the jacking operation progresses, but shall not excavate more than two feet in front of tunnel liner. Contractors shall reduce the two feet distance where material character results in excess loss of soil. Contractors shall remove excavated material through the tunnel liner. Once jacking is begun, continue operation without interruption to prevent the pipe from becoming firmly set in the embankment.
(b) Contractors shall perform tunneling such that the final tunnel liner position is within the following limits:
(1) Lateral alignment: within two percent of tunnel liner length.
(2) Vertical elevation: within one percent of tunnel liner vertical grade, provided that the final grade of the flow line is in the direction indicated on the drawings in article X of this chapter.
(Ord. No. 2005-09, app. B(02408, pt. 3), 4-25-2005)
1491:
(a) Contractors shall mechanically bore by use of a cutting head on a continuous auger. Tunnel liner shall be installed in the hole by jacking or other suitable methods. Contractors shall accomplish boring of hole and tunnel liner installation simultaneously. Contractors shall not permit boring to proceed more than one foot in front of tunnel liner.
(b) Contractors shall conduct initial boring using a pilot hole approximately two inches in diameter for the entire installation length. Contractors shall verify required line and grade and use pilot hole as the centerline of the larger hole to be bored. If rock is encountered in pilot hole, contractors shall withdraw equipment and relocate tunnel location. Contractors shall conduct pilot hole installation in revised location and repeat procedure. No extra payment will be considered for pilot hole installations that encounter rock and must be abandoned.
(c) Contractors shall perform tunneling such that the final tunnel liner position is within the following limits:
(1) Lateral alignment: within two percent of tunnel liner length.
(2) Vertical elevation: within one percent of tunnel liner vertical grade, provided that the final grade of the flow line is in the direction indicated on the drawings in article X of this chapter.
(Ord. No. 2005-09, app. B(02408, pt. 3), 4-25-2005)
1492:
(a) When installing tunnel liner by mining methods, contractors shall handle, maintain, and install liner plate sections in such manner as to avoid damage to plates and surface coating thereon. Contractors shall install liner plates immediately after excavated material is removed from the tunnel. Contractors shall not permit liner plate installation to fall more than 24 inches behind the tunnel working face. Contractors shall not leave more than 12 inches of unlined tunnel at the end of the day's operation.
(b) Contractors shall provide all necessary bracing bulkheads and/or shields required to ensure safety of persons and property. Contractors shall provide well-braced, temporary bulkhead against excavation face during each cessation of work while the heading is within 20 feet of railroad tracks or roadway pavement.
(c) Contractors shall pressure grout voids between excavated tunnel bore and liner plate at least daily as tunnel excavation and liner plate installation proceeds. In addition, contractors shall not extend liner plate installation more than ten feet without placing grout. Contractors shall introduce grout through all grout holes in tunnel liner plate at or near tunnel invert, continue grouting until grout mixture bleeds through grout holes located at tunnel crown. Contractors shall use grouting pressure sufficient to fill all voids.
(d) Contractors shall perform tunneling such that the final tunnel liner position is within 0.2 foot of specified position, both laterally and vertically.
(Ord. No. 2005-09, app. B(02408, pt. 3), 4-25-2005)
1493:
Should it become necessary to abandon a tunnel for any reason, contractors shall pressure grout the abandoned hole to prevent damage to surrounding earth and structures. When the tunnel liner is retained, fill entire tunnel with grout and pressure grout any voids about the tunnel liner exterior.
(Ord. No. 2005-09, app. B(02408, pt. 3), 4-25-2005)
1494:
(a) Contractors shall locate tunnels as indicated on the drawings in article X of this chapter.
(b) To facilitate construction, changes in tunnel location may be permitted. Proposed changes must be submitted by the contractor. Changes in location must be acceptable to the city, and any utility company or public agency having jurisdiction over the location.
(Ord. No. 2005-09, app. B(02408, pt. 3), 4-25-2005)
1495:
Contractors shall seal ends of the tunnel liner to prevent debris and moisture from entering the annular space between the carrier pipe and tunnel liner. For pipe tunnel liner, contractors shall provide the end seal consisting of flexible synthetic rubber boot conforming to ASTM C 923 or link seal penetration seal with insulating plastic plate, galvanized bolts and nuts, and EPDM rubber element manufactured by Thunderline Corporation.
(Ord. No. 2005-09, app. B(02408, pt. 3), 4-25-2005)
1496:
Construct vents for tunnel liners as indicated on the drawings in article X of this chapter or as required by any utility company or public agency having jurisdiction over the location.
(Ord. No. 2005-09, app. B(02408, pt. 3), 4-25-2005)
1500:
(a) The extent of trenching and backfilling is shown on the drawings in article X of this chapter.
(b) Trenching and backfilling operations include, but are not limited to, all earthwork associated with installation, modification, or abandonment of underground utilities and appurtenances, and restoration of damaged improvements.
(c) Related work specified elsewhere includes, but is not limited to, division 9 of this article, pertaining to route clearing.
(Ord. No. 2005-09, app. B(02204, pt. 1), 4-25-2005)
1501:
(a) Compliance with codes and standards. Contractors shall perform trenching and backfilling work in compliance with applicable requirements of governing authorities having jurisdiction where such requirements exceed those specified in this division.
(b) Sampling and testing. Contractors shall:
(1) Provide quality control testing during construction as necessary to assure the entire earthwork including all fill layers, subgrades, and bases meets contract requirements. Remove and reconstruct, or otherwise correct work, which falls below specified density or is outside other specified limits.
(2) Employ, at the contractor's expense, an independent testing laboratory to perform quality control testing during trenching and backfilling operations.

(Ord. No. 2005-09, app. B(02204, pt. 1), 4-25-2005)
1502:
(a) Contractors shall verify existing site grades to be substantially consistent with grades shown on the drawings before commencing work. Report any significant conflict in grades to the city before proceeding.
(b) Subsurface conditions presented, if any, are not intended as representations or warrants of continuity of such conditions between soil borings or pits. Data are made available for the convenience of the contractor who may perform additional test borings and other exploratory operations at the contractor's expense, provided such operations are acceptable to the city.

(2) Should unexpected piping or other utilities be encountered during excavation, consult the utility owner immediately for directions. Cooperate with the city and utility companies in keeping respective services and facilities in operation. Repair damaged utilities to satisfaction of utility owner.
(3) Not interrupt existing utilities serving facilities occupied and used by the city or others, except when permitted in writing by the city and then only after acceptable temporary utility services have been provided.
(4) Demolish and completely remove from site existing underground utilities indicated to be removed. Coordinate with utility companies for shut-off of services if lines are active.
(d) Traffic control. Contractors shall schedule and conduct work in a manner, which will minimize inconvenience to vehicular and pedestrian traffic. Flaggers, barricades, warning signs, warning lights, and other warning means shall be provided as appropriate. When flaggers are utilized, individuals must meet local and state requirements. Contractors shall maintain traffic on all roads and streets which must be crossed by trenching and making two separate cuts so that at least one traffic lane is open at all times. All traffic controls during construction must conform to Part VI of the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices, ANSI D6.1e.
(Ord. No. 2005-09, app. B(02204, pt. 1), 4-25-2005)
1505:
Stone rip rap shall be individual stones not less than six inches thick or 12 inches wide, not more than two cubic feet in volume and of proper shape to bring structures to accurate lines, shapes and elevations. Contractors shall provide stone free of rounded, or worn surfaces and also free of segregation, seams, cracks, pyrite intrusions and other defects tending to reduce weather resistance.
(Ord. No. 2005-09, app. B(02204, pt. 2), 4-25-2005)
1508:
Contractors shall protect persons and property by doing the following:
(1) Prior to commencing other work, accurately locate aboveground and belowground utilities and structures, which may be affected by the work, using whatever means be appropriate. Mark the location of existing utilities and structures, not otherwise readily visible, with flagging, stakes, barricades, or other suitable means.
(2) Barricade open excavations and post warning lights for safety of persons. Operate warning lights during hours from dusk to dawn each day.
(3) Protect structures, utilities, sidewalks, pavements, and other facilities immediately adjacent to excavations, from damage caused by settlement, lateral movement, undermining, washout and other hazards.
(4) Take precautions and provide necessary bracing and shoring to guard against movement or settlement of existing improvements or new construction. The contractor is entirely responsible for strength and adequacy of bracing and shoring, and for safety and support of construction from damage or injury caused by the lack thereof or by movement or settlement.
(5) Use work methods and provide temporary facilities as necessary to prevent washing, erosion, siltation or dust damage, or hazard to persons and property, within and outside the work area.
(6) Place excavated material compactly alongside of the trench, and keep such material trimmed up so as to present the least practicable inconvenience to the public. Where necessitated by traffic conditions, remove from the roadway the first material excavated from a working length of trench so that further excavation is immediately used for backfilling, and thereby avoid stockpiling of material upon the roadway. Afterward, return first excavated material if needed for final backfilling.
(7) Maintain all streets, sidewalks, crossings, fire hydrants, water and gas valves, fire alarm boxes, and other utilities accessible for their intended use except while the work is steadily advancing in the immediate vicinity of each such facility.
(8) Keep every drain, gutter, culvert, sewer, and surface drainage route encountered, open for both temporary and permanent flow unless other effective provision for drainage is made.
(9) Do not permit any hazardous condition to result from trenching and backfilling operations.
(Ord. No. 2005-09, app. B(02204, pt. 3), 4-25-2005)
1509:
(a) Contractors shall not bring explosives onto the site or use in work without prior written permission from authorities having jurisdiction.
(b) Contractors shall use explosives only as legally permitted and when other work methods are impractical.
(c) Contractors shall not permit explosives on the project site other than during the least practicable use period.
(d) Contractors shall assume sole responsibility for handling, storage, and use of any explosive materials.
(Ord. No. 2005-09, app. B(02204, pt. 3), 4-25-2005)
1510:
(a) Generally. Trenching consists of removal and disposal of material encountered to obtain required subgrade elevations, usually, but not necessarily limited to, that incidental to installation or modification of underground pipelines and appurtenances.
(b) Rock excavation. Rock excavation consists of removal and disposal of natural material encountered that cannot be excavated without continuous and systematic drilling and blasting or continuous use of a ripper or other special equipment. Intermittent drilling or blasting performed to increase production and unnecessary for excavation of material encountered will not be classified as rock excavation.
(c) Stability of excavation. Contractors shall ensure the stability of excavation by doing the following:
(1) Slope sides of excavations to comply with subpart P of part 1926 of the Occupational Safety and Health Act, as amended. Should any provision of a governing local code be more stringent than the preceding national standard, follow the local code. Shore and brace or use the trench box where sloping is not possible either because of space restrictions or stability of material excavated.
(2) Maintain sides and slopes of excavations in a safe condition until completion of backfilling.
(d) Shoring and bracing. Contractors shall provide shoring and bracing by doing the following:
(1) Provide portable trench boxes and materials for shoring and bracing, such as sheet piling, uprights, stringers and cross braces, in good serviceable condition.
(2) Maintain shoring and bracing and/or portable trench boxes in excavations regardless of the time period excavations will be open. Carry down shoring and bracing as excavation progresses.
(3) Provide trench boxes and/or shoring and bracing to comply with subpart P of part 1926 of the Occupational Safety and Health Act, as amended. Should any provision of a governing local code be more stringent than the preceding national standard, follow the local code.
(e) Dewatering. Contractors shall:
(1) Perform earthwork in a manner to prevent surface water and minimize subsurface or groundwater from flowing into excavations, and to prevent water from flooding the project work and surrounding area.
(2) Not allow water to accumulate in excavations. Remove water using dewatering methods, which will prevent softening of foundation bottoms, undercutting footings, and soil changes detrimental to stability of sub grades and foundations. Provide and maintain pumps, sumps, suction and discharge lines, and other dewatering system components necessary to convey water away from excavations.
(3) Limit opening of additional trench length to that which can be dewatered with available equipment or methods.
(4) Not use trenches as temporary drainage ditches.
(f) Material storage. When storing materials, contractors shall:
(1) Locate and retain materials away from edge of trench.
(2) Dispose of excess soil material and waste materials, such as unsatisfactory excavated soil material, trash and debris, as specified hereinafter.
(g) Excavating procedure. When excavating, contractors shall:
(1) Not extend excavation below or wider than that, which is necessary to construct work except as otherwise provided herein. Repair any unauthorized trenching as necessary to obtain an adequate sub grade as determined by the city.
(2) Limit open trench excavation to a maximum of 300 feet ahead of completed backfill.
(3) Where specific utility system elevations or depths are indicated on the drawings or elsewhere herein, accurately conform with such requirements. Otherwise, achieve a minimum earth and/or pavement cover of 30 inches above the top of underground utilities being constructed unless a greater cover is made necessary by easement or permit requirement, by maintaining a minimum clearance of 18 inches below any existing or proposed structure or channel, or by achieving proper alignment with existing or proposed facilities.
(4) Maintain a horizontal separation of at least ten feet between sanitary sewers and any existing or proposed water main. A sewer may be laid closer than ten feet to a water main if it is laid in a separate trench or it is laid in the same trench with the water main located at one side on a bench of undisturbed earth.
(5) Maintain a vertical separation of at least 18 inches between the crown of sanitary sewers and the invert of existing or proposed water mains with the sewer located below the water main. Where a vertical separation of 18 inches cannot be provided and the water main cannot be relocated to provide adequate clearance, center one full length of water main over the sewer so that both joints of the water main will be as far from the sewer as possible.
(6) Confine trench width from an elevation of one foot above the top of underground pipe to the trench bottom, to that minimum which is necessary to pipe laying operations, but do not exceed maximum trench width determined by pipe foundation requirements.
(7) Remove rock, masonry and concrete material to a distance of at least six inches from all parts of pipe and appurtenances being installed. Backfill and thoroughly compact, to proper trench bottom elevation, with select excavated material.
(8) Not mix excavated rock, masonry or concrete with backfill material placed within two feet of installed pipe, or within one foot of finished grade.
(h) Pavement removal. For pavement removal, contractors shall:
(1) Remove all pavement, including curb and gutter, sidewalk and the like, which must be disturbed by trenching operations.
(2) Saw cut edges of bituminous pavement. For concrete pavement, saw cut edges or remove and replace to the nearest joint.
(3) At sidewalks, curbs and gutters, and the like, remove the entire width of damaged sections.
(4) Extend pavement removal to the width required to accomplish trenching operations without damage to the edge of remaining pavement. Correct any edge damage, which occurs as requested by the city.
(i) Removal of unsatisfactory soil materials. To the extent required, contractors shall overexcavate those soil materials which are unsatisfactory in the opinion of the city and backfill with approved materials.
(Ord. No. 2005-09, app. B(02204, pt. 3), 4-25-2005)
1511:
(a) Generally. Contractors shall control soil compaction during construction providing the minimum percentage of density specified for each area classification.
(b) Percentage of maximum density requirements. Contractors shall achieve not less than the following percentages of maximum density of soil material compacted at optimum moisture content, for each layer of soil material-in-place as determined by ASTM D 698 (Standard Proctor) test procedures:
(1) Rights-of-way. For rights-of-way, contractors shall conform with the more stringent requirements of the permit issuing authority and the requirements herein.
(2) Roadways. Under and within five feet horizontal distance of traffic using surfaces, contractors shall compact each layer of backfill and fill material to 95 percent of maximum dry density.
(3) Walkways. Under and within two feet horizontal distance of paved walks, contractors shall compact the top six inches of subgrade and each layer of backfill and fill material to 95 percent of maximum dry density.
(4) Driveways and parking lots. Under and within two feet horizontal distance of traffic using surfaces, contractors shall compact each layer of backfill and fill material to 95 percent of maximum dry density.
(5) Lawns or unpaved areas. Contractors shall compact each layer of backfill or fill material to 85 percent of maximum dry density.
(6) Spoil areas. Contractors shall compact each layer of backfill or fill material to 85 percent of maximum dry density.
(c) Moisture control. To control moisture, contractors shall:
(1) Where a layer of soil material is too dry to achieve required compaction, uniformly apply water to the layer in such manner as to prevent excessive free water from appearing on the surface during or subsequent to compaction operations.
(2) Remove, dry and replace, or scarify and air dry in place, soil material that is too wet to achieve required compaction.
(Ord. No. 2005-09, app. B(02204, pt. 3), 4-25-2005)
1512:

The local stormwater design manual set forth in this article is meant to serve as a comprehensive guide to designing and implementing stormwater management controls and systems in the city. Additionally, the manual is designed to supplement the Georgia Stormwater Management Manual (GSMM), latest edition, which shall serve as the technical manual for design and specification of individual components within the system.
(Ord. No. 2005-09, app. D(1), 4-25-2005)
1544:
(a) Discharge rates—From new development projects.
(1) Development plans including site grading and drainage plans should be developed to minimize disruption of natural drainage patterns on properties. Additionally, no increases in stormwater runoff rates shall be allowed at any discharge point on the site. The baseline (predeveloped) conditions shall be a wooded undisturbed site regardless of whether any clearing has occurred in the past and shall model any depression storage and/or detention storage. The development shall be analyzed for the following storm events:
a. Two-year 24-hour design storm.
b. Five-year 24-hour design storm.
c. Ten-year 24-hour design storm.
d. Twenty-five-year 24-hour design storm.
e. Fifty-year 24-hour design storm.
f. One hundred-year 24-hour design storm.
(2) If the total area of the site (i.e., total property area) and the drainage area to each stormwater management facility is less than one acre, then a rainfall intensity based analysis (i.e., rational method) may be performed. If detention facilities are to be designed and constructed in series, the 24-hour storm criteria will apply regardless of the drainage area.
(b) Same—From redevelopment projects.
(1) Development plans including site grading and drainage plans should be developed to minimize disruption of natural drainage patterns on properties. Additionally, no increases in stormwater runoff rates shall be allowed at any discharge point on the site. The baseline conditions shall be based on an analysis of the stormwater discharge rates from the site in its existing condition and shall model any depression storage and/or detention storage. The development shall be analyzed for the following storm events:
a. Two-year 24-hour design storm.
b. Five-year 24-hour design storm.
c. Ten-year 24-hour design storm.
d. Twenty-five-year 24-hour design storm.
e. Fifty-year 24-hour design storm.
f. One hundred-year 24-hour design storm.
(2) If the total area of the site (i.e., total property area) and the drainage area to each stormwater management facility is less than one acre, then a rainfall intensity based analysis (i.e., rational method) may be performed. If detention facilities are to be designed and constructed in series, the 24-hour storm criteria will apply regardless of the drainage area.
(Ord. No. 2005-09, app. D(2.1), 4-25-2005)

(a) Pipes under roads and pavement.
(1) All pipes under roadways, parking lots and other surfaces designed for vehicular traffic; or designed to convey off-site stormwater through a project shall be constructed of reinforced concrete pipe (RCP) meeting state department of transportation standards. Any pipe that originates or terminates within or immediately adjacent (twice the depth of the pipe section adjacent to the roadway) to a pavement surface as defined above shall be continued to the next structure (i.e., manhole, inlet, headwall, etc.). Longitudinal pipes with diameters of 30 inches or smaller may be corrugated metal pipe (CMP) or high density polyethylene (HDPE) pipe if the depth of the pipe is four feet or less and if approved by special permission of the city engineer. Bedding standards for HDPE/CMP pipe shall be such that stone bedding (i.e., No. 57 stone) shall be placed to half of the pipe diameter for all depths greater than four feet and/or in accordance with manufacturers specifications whichever are greater. HDPE pipes must have a minimum of 24 inches of cover from the crown of the pipe unless prior approval of the city has been obtained.
(2) All CMP pipes shall be galvanized with a minimum of four ounces of galvanization per square foot and be 14 gauge or heavier construction. Those areas where a high ground water table exists or soil corrosivity is excessive as determined by the city only RCP may be utilized. The city may at its discretion require soil tests to be provided at the owner's expense to determine corrosivity of the soils and the presence of groundwater.
(b) Pipes not under roads and pavement.
(1) Pipes not under roadways, parking lots and other surfaces meant for vehicular traffic shall be constructed of RCP, HDPE, or CMP meeting state department of transportation standards and approved by the local jurisdictional authority. Bedding standards for HDPE/CMP pipe shall be such that stone bedding (i.e., No. 57 stone) shall be placed to half of the pipe diameter for all depths greater than four feet and/or in accordance with manufacturer's specifications, whichever is greater. HDPE pipes must have a minimum of 24 inches of cover from the crown of the pipe unless prior approval of the city has been obtained.
(2) All CMP pipes shall be galvanized with a minimum of four ounces of galvanization per square foot and be 14 gauge or heavier construction. Those areas where a high ground water table exists or soil corrosivity is excessive as determined by the city only RCP may be utilized. The city may at its discretion require soil tests to be provided at the owner's expense to determine corrosivity of the soils and the presence of groundwater.
(c) Channels. All channels must be protected from erosion through the use of rip rap, concrete, erosion control matting or similar method acceptable to the city. All channel side slopes shall have a three-foot horizontal to one-foot vertical (3:1) slope or less.
(d) Inlets. All inlets shall be constructed of materials and methods approved by the state department of transportation and designs preapproved by the city.

The following words, terms and phrases, when used in this chapter, shall have the meanings ascribed to them in this section, except where the context clearly indicates a different meaning:
Buffer means a portion of a tract which is set aside to provide a perceived or actual visual separation between the use on the tract and abutting tracts or through the use of natural vegetation or other means including replanting or the provision of supplemental plantings or other visual screening elements or noise attenuation devices.
Caliper is the measurement of a nursery grown tree six inches from the ground. For multi-stem trees it shall be the measure of the largest stem six inches above split.
Canopy tree means a tree which attains a mature height of at least 40 feet and a spread of at least one-half its height. All trees included in this category shall have a distinctive crown.
City administrator means the administrator of the City of Fairburn, Georgia.
Clearing means an activity which removes or disturbs the soil or vegetative cover, including trees.
Crown dripline means a vertical line extending from the outer surface of a tree's branch tips to the ground.
Deciduous tree means any tree which drops its leaves at the end of the growing season.
Diameter at breast height (DBH) means a standard measure of tree size, and is the trunk diameter measured in inches at a height of four and one-half feet above the ground. If a tree splits into multiple trunks below four and one-half feet, then each trunk is measured as a separate tree. A tree which splits into multiple trunks above four and one-half feet is measured as a single tree at four and one-half feet.
Dripline area means the total area underneath a tree, or grouping of trees, which would encompass all driplines.
Evergreen means any tree which retains its green foliage throughout the year.
Floodplain, 100-year, means those lands subject to flooding, which have at least a one percent probability of flooding occurrence in any calendar year; and specifically, the floodplain as shown on the flood boundary and floodway map as prepared by the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA).
Land disturbance permit means a permit issued pursuant to chapter 65, article II, pertaining to soil erosion and sedimentation.
Land disturbing activity means any land change which may result in soil erosion from water or wind and the movement of sediment into state water or onto lands within the state, including, but not limited to, clearing, dredging, grading, excavating, transporting and filling of land, other than federal lands, and which requires issuance of a land disturbance permit.
Landscape area means an area set aside for the installation, cultivation and maintenance of native and/or ornamental plant material.
Landscape irrigation system requirements means those requirements for same set forth in section 59-29.
Landscaping means any additions to the natural features of a plot of ground to restore construction disturbance and to make it more attractive, as by adding lawns, trees and shrubs, etc. to the natural environment.
Natural vegetation means a generally undisturbed, maintenance-free, self-perpetuating stand of vegetation comprised of indigenous shrubs, flowers, wild grasses and trees.
Natural vegetation area means the areas within the boundaries of a given lot which is devoted to the preservation of natural vegetation.
Protection area means all land which falls outside the buildable area of a parcel, all areas of the parcel required to remain in open space, the dripline area beneath a tree or clusters of trees to be retained, and/or all areas required as landscaping strips or buffers according to the provisions of the city zoning regulations contained in chapter 80, as may from time to time be amended, or conditions of zoning approval.
Shrub means a woody plant of relatively low profile with a mature height of one to six feet, distinguished from a tree by having several stems rather than a single trunk.
Specimen tree or stand means any tree or grouping of trees which has been determined to be of high value because of its species, size, age or location. General criteria for the determination of specimen trees or stands are as follows:
(1) Any deciduous canopy tree the DBH of which equals or exceeds 30 inches.
(2) Any evergreen canopy tree the DBH of which equals or exceeds 24 inches.
(3) Any understory tree the DBH of which equals or exceeds ten inches.
(4) Any tree which has a significant historical value and can be documented through historical records or otherwise.
Timber reforestation means the planting of seedling trees on a site on which an approved commercial timber harvest has been completed.
Tree density standard means the minimum number of tree density units per acre which must be maintained or achieved on a property after development.
Tree density unit means a credit assigned to a tree, based on the diameter of the tree, in accordance with tables contained in this chapter.
Tree diameter means the widest cross sectional dimension of a tree trunk measured at diameter breast height (DBH), or caliper for new trees.
Tree removal permit means a written permit given by the city administrator to a person, public or private, that the tree protection plan, landscape plan and application, as submitted or revised, has been approved by the appropriate authorities under this chapter.
Understory tree means any tree or woody plant which is of a lesser height and spread than surrounding evergreens or deciduous trees but which still provides shade and a degree of the protection to the earth and vegetation beneath it.
Zoning buffer is a portion of a tract which is permanently set aside to provide a perceived or actual visual (or horizontal spatial) separation between the use on the tract and abutting tracts through the use of natural vegetation or other means including replanting or the provision of supplemental plantings or other visual screening elements or noise attenuation devices.
(Code 1966, § 24A-1; Ord. No. 92-06, § 1, 8-10-1992; Ord. No. 2012-15, § 1, 12-10-2012; Ord. of 2-24-2020, § 2)

(1) Credit for existing trees to be retained shall be calculated by multiplying the number of trees (by diameter) times the units assigned in the following Table 74-A. Credit shall be given all trees retained on a property having a diameter of three inches or more, except trees located in a zoning buffer and/or floodplain. Zoning buffers and floodplain area shall not be calculated in density acreage nor shall existing trees in these areas be utilized to fulfill density requirements.
(2) Credit for new trees proposed on the site shall be calculated by multiplying the number of trees (by diameter) times the units assigned in the following Table 74-B. Credit shall be given all new trees on a property except for new trees of less than one-inch caliper and new trees planted in a required zoning buffer. Seedling trees of less than one-inch caliper may only be used for timber reforestation of areas greater than one-half acre.

a. A total tree density credit not to exceed twice the units shown on Table 74-A, may be granted by the city administrator or his designee for existing trees to be retained which have greater value as outstanding specimen trees or having historic value or being a rare or unique species.
b. Existing trees to be retained within a minimum yard area (as required by the applicable zoning district) may be granted a bonus credit up to 50 percent of the units assigned in Table 74-A unless the tree is located within a required zoning buffer.

1594:
The following guidelines and standards shall apply to trees proposed to be retained for credit toward meeting the minimum required tree density standard on a property:
(1) Tree protection areas. The root system within the dripline is generally considered to be the critical root zone. To protect these critical root zones, a tree protection area shall be established around each tree or group of trees to be retained.
a. The tree protection area shall include no less than the total area beneath the tree canopy as defined by the dripline of the tree or group of trees collectively. In some instances, a larger area than the dripline area may be required to be designated as a tree protection area as determined by the state forestry commission or the city engineer.
b. Layout of the project site utility and grading plans shall avoid disturbance of the tree protection areas.
c. Construction site activities such as parking, materials storage, concrete washout, burnhole placement, etc., shall be arranged so as to prevent disturbances within tree protection areas.
(2) Protective barriers.
a. Protective tree fencing shall be installed between tree protection areas and areas proposed to be cleared, graded or otherwise disturbed on the site, prior to any land disturbance.
b. All tree protection areas shall be designated as such with "tree protection area" signs posted in addition to the required protective fencing. Signs requiring subcontractor cooperation and compliance with tree protection standards shall be placed at site entrances.
c. All tree protection areas must be protected from soil sedimentation intrusion through the use of silt fence or other acceptable measures placed upslope from the tree protection area.
d. All protective tree fencing and all erosion control barriers must be installed prior to and maintained throughout the land disturbance and construction process, and shall not be removed until final landscaping is installed or final plat approval.
(3) Encroachment. If encroachment into a tree protection area occurs which causes irreparable damage to the trees, the tree protection plan and landscape plan shall be revised to compensate for the loss. Under no circumstances shall the developer be relieved of responsibility for compliance with the provisions of this chapter, nor shall plan revision activities stop the city administrator or his designee from instituting action for violation of this chapter.
(4) Fill dirt. It is prohibited to place fill dirt in any tree protection areas or around any replacement trees.
(5) Biodegradable debris. All biodegradable debris, including but not limited to stumps, limbs or tops of trees, shall be properly disposed of and shall not be buried on site.
(Code 1966, § 24A-11; Ord. No. 92-06, § 1, 8-10-1992; Ord. No. 2012-15, § 1, 12-10-2012)

1596:
The following are the requirements and guidelines for tree protection to be followed during the grading and construction process:
(1) All individual stand-alone trees to be retained on the site must be marked with orange engineering tape tied around the trunk of the tree at a height of five feet above the ground.
(2) The tree protection area (dripline area) of stand-alone trees and stands of trees will be marked with standard tree protection fencing (orange). At least two "tree protection area" signs shall be posted at each individual tree protection area. No construction activities will be allowed within the tree protection area.
(3) The tree protection area shall be maintained as a natural vegetation area or an area landscaped with shrubs or understory trees when possible and mulched with either pine straw or shredded wood fiber. The seeding or sodding of grass in the tree protection area is to be avoided.
(4) Credit for existing trees shall not be granted if there is any proposed or actual encroachment into dripline of the tree(s). If existing trees are to be saved, special attention shall be given to the protection of the dripline area (roots) and pruning of the tree may be required to reduce potential damage from stress. In situations such as this, the state forestry commission should be contacted for technical assistance.
(5) Utilities shall not be run through a tree protection area unless they are tunneled at a depth of 24 inches in a manner which will damage as little of the root system as possible.
(6) If it is determined that irreparable damage has occurred to a tree or trees within a designated tree protection area, as determined by the city administrator, his designee or the state forestry commission, then it shall be the responsibility of the owner to remove and replace the tree or trees and guarantee survival.
(Code 1966, § 24A-13; Ord. No. 92-06, § 1, 8-10-1992; Ord. No. 2012-15, § 1, 12-10-2012)
1597:
In some cases, tree replacement (recompense planting) will be necessary to fulfill the tree density requirement. Although the preservation of existing trees is important, it is also important to replenish the rural/urban forest as development occurs with new trees to ensure the presence of trees for generations to come. The following are the requirements for tree replacement at the conclusion of the construction process:
(1) All planting shall be as designated on the approved landscape plan.
a. New trees proposed to be planted for credit toward meeting the minimum required tree density standard in a property shall comply with the following guidelines and standards:
1. The spacing of new trees must be compatible with spatial site limitations and with responsible consideration towards species size when mature.
2. Trees selected for replacement must be quality specimens free of disease, injury or infestation and must be ecologically compatible with the specifically intended growing area and provided in accordance with standards established in the American Standard for Nursery Stock (ANSI 260.1-2004).
(2) A 50 percent mix of replacement canopy and replacement understory trees shall be maintained. Canopy trees shall be a minimum 2½" caliper. Understory trees shall be a minimum 1½" caliper.
(3) Replacement trees shall not be planted within 15 feet of any structure or within five feet of a paved driveway unless they are replacement understory trees.
(4) In the event that new trees proposed to be planted to achieve the tree density standard are not installed upon application for a certificate of occupancy or final plat approval (as appropriate), then a performance bond or other acceptable surety in an amount equal to 300 percent (unit cost plus unit installed plus unit guaranteed) of the cost of the new trees shall be posted in accordance with performance bonding requirements.
(5) Upon final installation of landscaping planted under the requirements of this chapter, and following acceptance by the city administrator or his designee, the owner shall warrant the landscaping and provide for the replacement of that which does not survive.

(1) Words and phrases defined in this chapter shall be interpreted as defined herein without regard to other meanings in common or ordinary use, unless the context of the word indicates otherwise.
(2) Words or phrases not defined herein shall be interpreted as defined in the zoning ordinance set forth in chapter 80, as defined in the development standards of the city, as defined in the soil erosion and sediment control ordinance set forth in chapter 65, article II, as defined in the sewer use ordinance set forth in chapter 59, or the floodplain management/flood damage prevention ordinance set forth in chapter 68, or landscaping as set forth in chapter 74, as applicable to the use of the word or phrase within the context of this chapter.

(b) Definitions. The following words, terms and phrases, when used in this chapter, shall have the meanings ascribed to them in this subsection, except where the context clearly indicates a different meaning:
Concept plat means a drawing that shows the overall concept of a proposed development, as further defined in these regulations.
Easement means legal authorization for a specified purpose by a property owner for the use of any designated part of the real property by another entity.
Final plat means a finished drawing of a subdivision showing completely and accurately all legal and boundary information and certifications required by these regulations and conforming to the Georgia Plat Act.
Health department means the health department of the county.
Lot means a portion of a subdivision, or any other tract or parcel of land, intended as a unit for transfer of ownership or for development or both.
Plat means a map or drawing indicating the subdivision, resubdivision, or recombination of land.
Preliminary plat means a drawing that shows the perimeter boundary, topography, lot layout arrangement, street layout, and other features of a proposed subdivision, as specified in these regulations.
Road. The term "road" is used interchangeably with the term "street."
Sketch plat. Refer to "concept plat."
Street, private, means an accessway, other than a driveway, similar to and having the same function as a public street, providing access to more than one property, but held in private ownership.
Street, public, means a right-of-way dedicated to and accepted by the city for vehicular traffic or over which the city may hold a prescriptive easement for public access, and including designated and numbered U.S. and state highways. For purposes of these regulations, the term "public street" shall be limited to those, which afford a direct means of vehicular access to abutting property, and exclude limited access highways which abut a property but from which direct access may not be allowed under any circumstances.
Subdivider means any person dividing or proposing to divide land so as to constitute a subdivision as herein defined.
Subdivision.
(1) When used as a verb, the term "subdivision" means any division or redivision of a lot, tract, or parcel, regardless of its existing or future use, into two or more lots, tracts, or parcels. The term "subdivision" shall mean the act or process of dividing property.

1632:
The steps of the concept plat review process are as follows:
(1) Step 1. The developer of a proposed subdivision shall meet with the development coordinator to discuss what is required for concept plat approval in terms of documents, fees, and schedules.
(2) Step 2. The developer shall submit to the city a complete concept plat application package, and that submittal shall be logged in by the administrative assistant.
(3) Step 3. The concept plat application package is carefully checked by the development coordinator to determine whether or not it is complete. If it is incomplete, it needs to be returned to the developer with an explanation of why it is incomplete and what must be done to make it complete. The developer will then begin the process again with step 2 set forth in subsection (2) and no additional fee will be required.
(4) Step 4. If the concept plat application package is complete, it will be accepted by the development coordinator; the date of acceptance will be noted; and the concept plat will be distributed for staff comments. For every submittal, copies shall be provided to the director of community development, the city engineer, the property manager, the fire marshal and the city's engineering consultant. Copies will also be provided to other staff members on an as-needed basis. The staff shall have at least ten working days for review of the concept plat, preparing comments and submitting a report to the development coordinator.
(5) Step 5. After the staff review period, the development coordinator shall schedule a staff review meeting. At least five working days prior to that meeting, all staff members shall be provided a copy of all staff reports.
(6) Step 6. At the staff review meeting, all reports shall be reviewed and all differences resolved. All notes, memos and documents concerning that meeting shall be kept in the project file.
(7) Step 7. The results of the staff meeting shall be combined into a single staff report by the development coordinator. That report shall be reviewed and approved by all participating staff members prior to it being released to the developer.
(8) Step 8. If the staff report concludes the concept plat can be placed on a planning and zoning commission agenda, it should be scheduled for the next available regular meeting. If the report concludes the concept plat is not acceptable, the concept plat shall be returned to the developer with an explanation of why it was found to not be acceptable, and with instructions as to what needs to be done to make it acceptable. The developer will then begin the process again at step 2 set forth in subsection (2) and a new plat review fee will be required.
(9) Step 9. The development coordinator shall forward the approved staff report and the concept plat application package to the planning and zoning commission members at least five calendar days prior to the scheduled meeting of the commission. If the report cannot be provided to the members at least five calendar days prior to the meeting, the matter must be rescheduled to a subsequent regular meeting.
(10) Step 10. The planning and zoning commission shall review the concept plat and the staff report at the scheduled regular meeting. If the commission approves the concept plat, the developer will be authorized to proceed with the preparation of a preliminary plat that will be based on the approved concept and be in accordance with all conditions and agreements included in the commission's action to approve the concept. If approval of the concept plat is denied or tabled by the commission, the developer shall be provided with the reasons for denial or tabling and an explanation of what will be required to secure approval. In this event, the developer will begin the process again with step 2 set forth in subsection (2) and a new plat review fee will be required.
(Ord. No. 2005-4(1), § 5.3, 2-28-2005; Ord. No. 2012-15, § 1, 12-10-2012)

(a) Procedural steps. The steps of the site development plan review process are as follows:
(1) Step 1. The developer of a proposed subdivision shall meet with the development coordinator to discuss what is required for site development plan approval in terms of documents, fees, and schedules.
(2) Step 2. The developer shall submit to the city a complete site development plan application package, and that submittal shall be logged in by the administrative assistant.
(3) Step 3. The site development plan application package shall be carefully checked by the development coordinator to determine whether or not it is complete. If it is incomplete, it needs to be returned to the developer with an explanation of why it is incomplete and what must be done to make it complete. The developer will then begin the process again with step 2 set forth in subsection (a)(2) and no additional fee will be required.
(4) Step 4. If the site development plan application package is complete, it will be accepted by the development coordinator; the date of acceptance will be noted; and the site development plans will be distributed for staff comments. For every submittal, copies shall be provided to the director of community development, the city engineer, the property manager, the fire marshal and the city's engineering consultant. Copies will also be provided to other staff members on an as-needed basis. The staff shall have at least ten working days for review of the site development plans, preparing comments and submitting a report to the development coordinator.
(5) Step 5. After the staff review period, the development coordinator shall schedule a staff review meeting. At least five working days prior to that meeting, all staff members shall be provided a copy of all staff reports.
(6) Step 6. At the staff review meeting, all reports shall be reviewed and all differences resolved. All notes, memos and documents concerning that meeting shall be kept in the project file.
(7) Step 7. The results of the staff meeting shall be combined into a single staff report by the development coordinator. That report shall be reviewed and approved by all participating staff members prior to it being released to the developer.
(8) Step 8. If the staff report concludes the site development plans can be approved, the city engineer shall approve two identical sets of plans, one for the developer and one for the city. The developer shall then make ten copies of the approved set for the city, along with one 11-inch by 17-inch set. The developer shall keep one copy of the approved set on the construction site at all times.
(9) Step 9. Upon request, after approval on the site development plans, the city engineer shall issue a permit to install the erosion control facilities and the tree-save fence in accordance with the approved plans. A fee is required for this permit.
(10) Step 10. Upon request, the staff shall inspect the property to determine whether or not the erosion control facilities and tree-save fence were installed properly. This inspection shall take place within three working days of the request. If the installation is approved, the developer may next request a permit to clear the unprotected trees and grade the land.
(11) Step 11. If the installation is not approved, the developer shall be informed in writing of what needs to be done to secure approval, and then begin the process again with step 10 set forth in subsection (a)(10). A reinspection fee shall be required.
(12) Step 12. After approval of the erosion control facilities and tree-save fence, the developer may request that the city engineer issue a permit to clear and grade the property in accordance with the approved plans. A fee is required for this permit.
(13) Step 13. Upon request, the staff shall inspect the property to determine whether or not the clearing and grading were done properly. This inspection shall take place within five working days of the request. If the clearing and grading are approved, the developer may next request a final site development permit.
(14) Step 14. If the clearing and grading are not approved, the developer shall be informed in writing of what needs to be done to secure approval, and then begin the process again with step 13 set forth in subsection (a)(13). A reinspection fee shall be required.
(15) Step 15. After approval of the clearing and grading, the developer may request a final site development permit from the city engineer.
(16) Step 16. Upon request, the staff shall inspect the property to determine whether or not the site has been developed in accordance with the approved plans. Also, the developer shall submit for review and approval all test results and certifications that are required to demonstrate satisfactory construction and adherence to all codes, ordinances and development standards. On the basis of the site inspection and the review of the supporting documentation, the staff shall determine whether or not the construction work is acceptable. This determination shall be made within ten working days of the request. If it is determined that the construction is satisfactory, the city engineer will authorize the preparation of a final plat.
(17) Step 17. If the construction is not approved, the developer shall be informed in writing of what needs to be done to secure approval, and then begin the process again with step 16 set forth in subsection (a)(16). A reinspection fee shall be required.
(b) Approval of changes to plan. If the developer wishes to make any substantive change to the construction plans at any time during the process, that change must first be approved by the planning and zoning commission in accordance with the preliminary plat review process.
(c) Staff inspections and progress reports. Staff inspections will be performed on a regular basis during the construction process to assure conformance with the approved plans and specifications; and regular progress reports will be presented to the planning and zoning commission and the mayor and council.
